title: manifest.ts loadManifest still wraps fs.readFile errors in a misleading 'not found' message
description: Iter-1 R3-001 carried over. The catch block around fs.readFile rethrows a fixed 'Deployment manifest not found at <path>' message regardless of the underlying errno (EACCES, EISDIR, EMFILE all become 'not found'). The original error is dropped — no `cause`, no errno, no console.error. parseManifest was correctly extracted in iter-2 (good) but loadManifest's I/O error path was not improved.
impact: Operator with a permissions issue gets pointed at `pnpm deploy-all`, which won't fix it. Same harm as iter-1; loadManifest is now Node-only (used by tests / CLI tooling) so the production browser path is unaffected, but unit-test debugging is still degraded.
recommendation: Discriminate on `(err as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code` — only claim 'not found' for ENOENT, otherwise emit `Deployment manifest at ${path} unreadable: ${code}` with `{ cause: err }`.

title: manifest.ts loadManifest JSON.parse still unguarded; malformed JSON throws raw SyntaxError
description: Iter-1 R3-002 NOT FIXED. After fs.readFile succeeds, line 105 calls `JSON.parse(raw) as unknown` with no try/catch. parseManifest validates the shape AFTER parse, but a malformed JSON payload (truncated mid-write by `pnpm deploy-all`, BOM, accidental edit) still throws a raw `SyntaxError: Unexpected token ... in JSON at position N` with no manifest path and no bootstrap hint.
impact: AC1.2 actionable-error guarantee is bypassed for the malformed-JSON case. The only inputs that reach the validator are objects that already parsed; the parse step itself is a silent crash hazard. The same issue exists in main.tsx (response.json() also unguarded — see R3-018).
recommendation: Wrap line 105 in try/catch and rethrow as `Deployment manifest at ${manifestPath} is not valid JSON: ${(err as Error).message}. ${BOOTSTRAP_HINT}`.
evidence:
const parsed = JSON.parse(raw) as unknown;
  return parseManifest(parsed, manifestPath);

title: main.tsx silently no-ops when #root element is missing
description: Iter-1 R3-006 NOT FIXED. If `document.getElementById('root')` returns null (broken index.html, hot-reload race, mismatched id), the `if (root)` guard silently skips createRoot/render — blank page, no console error, no diagnostic.
impact: Blank page with zero diagnostic. Low because index.html is correct today, but the silent-skip default is wrong for a fatal mounting precondition.
recommendation: Replace the silent `if (root)` with `if (!root) throw new Error('main.tsx: #root missing in index.html')` or at minimum `console.error(...)`.

title: rpc() still does not check response.ok; non-2xx responses produce confusing JSON-parse errors
description: Iter-1 R3-009 NOT FIXED. The `rpc()` helper still calls `await response.json()` without first asserting `response.ok` or `response.status`. A 502/503 from the Sui RPC port, a 404 from a wrong path, or an HTML error page from a misconfigured proxy will throw `SyntaxError: Unexpected token < in JSON at position 0` rather than the actionable RPC-unreachable error AC1.1/T-020 promise.
impact: Sandbox-down or sandbox-restart-mid-cycle (a contract-acknowledged failure mode) surfaces as opaque JSON parse errors instead of the inline 'Sui RPC unreachable; run pnpm deploy-all' message. The error then propagates through the new Promise.allSettled in App.tsx as a per-pool error, but its content is non-actionable.
recommendation: Before `await response.json()`, add `if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Sui RPC ${method} returned HTTP ${response.status} from ${rpcUrl}. Verify the sandbox is running.`);`. Also wrap the json() call in try/catch.

title: rpc() still does not handle network-level fetch rejection (DNS, connection refused)
description: Iter-1 R3-010 NOT FIXED. The fetch() call has no try/catch; the most common sandbox-down case (port closed → `TypeError: Failed to fetch`) propagates verbatim. The error message names neither the RPC URL nor the bootstrap recipe, so the user sees only 'TypeError: Failed to fetch' inside App.tsx's per-pool error banner.
impact: The most user-visible failure mode (sandbox not running) gets the least actionable error. Now made worse by iter-2: Promise.allSettled in App.tsx wraps the rejection so the user sees one identical, opaque 'Failed to fetch' line per pool, multiplying noise without adding signal.
recommendation: Wrap fetch in try/catch and rethrow with a wrapped, actionable message that includes rpcUrl and the bootstrap hint, attaching the original via `{ cause: err }`.

title: rpc() still casts result to T without checking env.result is defined
description: Iter-1 R3-011 NOT FIXED. After the env.error guard, `return env.result as T` proceeds even if env.result is undefined. Downstream callers (resolvePoolInnerFields, traverseBigVector, buildQueryEventsFn) then read fields off undefined/empty objects via `?.` chains and ?? defaults, silently producing empty books / no fills with no error signal.
impact: An aberrant or partial JSON-RPC response (proxy injection, edge-case server impl) results in silent empty data instead of an explicit error. Combined with the new fallback chains in resolvePoolInnerFields (returns null → buildPoolInnerState skipped → empty Book) the path is now even more silent than in iter-1.
recommendation: After the env.error branch, add `if (env.result === undefined) throw new Error(\`${method} returned no result and no error\`);`.

title: computeMarketStats BigInt(orderId) and Number(quantity) still unguarded against malformed inputs
description: Iter-1 R3-013 NOT FIXED. decodeAskPrice / decodeBidPrice still call `BigInt(orderId)` with no try/catch; a non-numeric order_id (chain-shape drift, dataLayer fallback string '0' from R3-006-style undefined) throws synchronous SyntaxError. Number(o.quantity) on lines 51/56 still has no Number.isFinite guard; non-numeric quantities silently become NaN and every NaN level then fails `lvl.price >= lo && lvl.price <= hi` (NaN comparisons are always false), so depth silently drops affected levels with no warning.
impact: BigInt throw is a hard-crash path. Now fully reachable in production via the new fetchSinglePoolStats wiring. The new traverseBigVector path (line 205) defaults order_id to `String(orderFields['order_id'] ?? keys[i] ?? '0')` — if orderFields has no order_id and keys[i] is missing, '0' is passed to BigInt(), which decodes to a sentinel price of 0 silently (BigInt('0') doesn't throw, but produces meaningless price). Either crash or silent-zero, both bad.
recommendation: Wrap order-id decode in try/catch and skip orders that fail (with optional console.warn). After Number(), guard `Number.isFinite(qty)` and skip non-finite levels.

title: aggregateFills coerces fill price/quantity via Number() with no NaN guard
description: Iter-1 R3-014 NOT FIXED. aggregateFills sums `Number(f.baseQuantity)` into volume24h and casts `Number(sorted[last].price)` for lastPrice without guarding against NaN. A single malformed fill record (chain-shape drift, missing field) poisons the whole day's volume (NaN + N = NaN for the rest of the loop) and lastPrice silently becomes NaN. PoolCard's fmt sentinel masks the symptom — user sees '—' for ALL trades when only one was malformed.
impact: Single bad fill corrupts whole-day volume. Silent: '—' looks identical to 'no trades'. Now reachable via the live data layer (no longer behind the iter-1 stub).
recommendation: `const q = Number(f.baseQuantity); if (Number.isFinite(q)) volume24h += q;` and similarly for price. Optional: count and surface malformedFills.

title: fetchFills loop still has no upper bound on pagination; misbehaving RPC could spin forever
description: Iter-1 R3-015 NOT FIXED. fetchFills uses `while (true)` with three break conditions but no maximum-iteration safety bound. If queryEvents returns hasNextPage:true indefinitely while always returning data old-but-not-quite (so neither MAX_FILLS nor crossedWindow fires) or returns the same cursor, fetchFills hangs forever and App stays in 'loading' status with no signal.
impact: Hung loading state with no timeout. Combined with the new setInterval refresh (App.tsx line 94), a hung fetchFills will block subsequent refresh cycles' Promise.allSettled too, since each interval awaits its own batch.
recommendation: Add hard iteration cap: `for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++)` and throw 'queryEvents pagination exceeded N pages without satisfying stop conditions' if reached. Also detect cursor-no-advance.

title: fetchFills still does not handle queryEvents returning non-array data
description: Iter-1 R3-016 NOT FIXED. fillFetcher.ts assumes response.data is iterable. dataLayer.ts buildQueryEventsFn does defend with `result.data ?? []`, so the production path through is safe — but the type signature of QueryEventsFn allows a custom impl returning `data: undefined` (not impossible given R3-006 means rpc() can return undefined). The `for (const ev of response.data)` then throws `TypeError: response.data is not iterable`.
impact: Edge-case crash with non-actionable error message. Lower risk than iter-1 because dataLayer.ts now defends, but the contract is fragile — any new caller of QueryEventsFn must remember to defend.
recommendation: `if (!Array.isArray(response.data)) throw new Error('queryEvents returned non-array data field');` at top of loop body.
evidence:
for (const ev of response.data) {
      if (ev.poolId !== poolId) continue;

title: PoolCard fmt() uses String(value) — fine numerics render as scientific notation
description: Iter-1 R3-017 NOT FIXED. fmt() returns `String(value)` for finite numbers; very small or very large values render as scientific notation (e.g. '1.23e-8') which a non-technical user might misread as the sentinel. Now reachable: iter-1 the data layer was stubbed to zeros so this was hidden; iter-2 wires real chain values where small mid-prices and depth-per-tick values are plausible.
impact: Cosmetic / latent UX bug. Not load-bearing for any AC.
recommendation: Mirror sparkline's toFixed approach: `value.toLocaleString(undefined, { maximumFractionDigits: 6 })` or pin per-field toFixed.

title: Vite middleware 404 body discarded by main.tsx; user sees less actionable message
description: vite.config.ts (lines 38-45) catches the readFile error and returns a 404 with body `{"error": "localnet.json not found at <abs-path>. Run pnpm deploy-all from the deepbook-sandbox repo."}`. main.tsx checks `!response.ok` and throws its own message ('not reachable at /localnet.json. Run pnpm deploy-all ...') — the body is never read. The middleware took the trouble to compute and emit the absolute disk path and surface the precise reason, but main.tsx throws all that information away and substitutes a generic message. User loses the absolute path that would help them diagnose 'is the sandbox checked out at the expected location?'.
impact: AC1.2 'actionable error pointing at the bootstrap recipe' is partially satisfied — the message names `pnpm deploy-all` — but loses the per-environment specificity (the actual disk path the middleware tried) that would make the error truly actionable for a misconfigured workspace. Two messages, one less informative than the other; the less-informative one wins.
recommendation: Have main.tsx read the response body on !response.ok and prefer the server's error message if present: `const body = await response.json().catch(() => null); throw new Error(body?.error ?? defaultMessage);`.

title: main.tsx fetch + response.json() unguarded against network or parse errors
description: main.tsx loadManifest does NOT wrap `fetch(MANIFEST_URL)` in try/catch (network failure → raw TypeError) nor `await response.json()` (malformed JSON → raw SyntaxError). The Vite middleware can in principle return malformed JSON if the manifest file itself is malformed (the middleware does no parse-validation, just reads bytes and serves). A truncated/corrupted manifest then surfaces as `SyntaxError: Unexpected token...` directly into App's error UI without any indication this is a manifest-shape problem.
impact: AC1.1/AC1.2 actionable-error guarantee bypassed in the browser path for the same two failure modes parseManifest now defends in the validation step. Defense-in-depth gap: the validator handles bad shapes, the fetch wrapper handles HTTP non-2xx, but the JSON decode in between is unguarded.
recommendation: Wrap `await response.json()` in try/catch and rethrow as 'Deployment manifest at /localnet.json is not valid JSON: ...'. Same pattern fixes the analogous problem in manifest.ts (R3-002).

title: computeMarketStats falls back to broken decodeBidPrice when Order.price is not injected by data layer
description: Iter-2 introduced `Order.price?` to let the data layer inject the real OrderInfo event price (preferred over order_id bit-decoding, which is documented as broken for bids in chain-shape.md line 136). However, dataLayer.ts.traverseBigVector (lines 196-209) does NOT populate `Order.price` — it reads only order_id, quantity, filled_quantity, status from the slice. The synthesis-notes explicitly say 'data layer can inject the real OrderInfo event price' as if this were done, but the code path simply omits the assignment. Result: in production, `o.price !== undefined` is always false for bids, so `decodeBidPrice(o.order_id)` runs — and that decoder is documented as 'tautologically correct against test fixtures but wrong against real chain order_ids' (marketStats.ts line 53-54 admits this in a comment).
impact: Bid prices in the deployed app will be wrong silently. Mid-price (computed as (bestBid+bestAsk)/2) becomes garbage. Spread becomes garbage. Depth-at-+/-1% sums random ladder levels relative to a meaningless mid. This is the worst class of silent failure: numbers render, the UI looks healthy, but every bid-side computation is wrong. AC1.4's invariant `bestBid <= mid <= bestAsk` is enforced only against fixtures, not against live chain data; against real bids, mid and spread are computed off bogus best-bid values. The iter-1 'silent stub' problem has been replaced by a 'silent garbage' problem at one layer deeper.
recommendation: Either (a) wire dataLayer.ts to fetch the OrderInfo / OrderPlaced events for each Order in the book and inject `price` from event.parsedJson.price, or (b) fix decodeBidPrice's bit math to match real chain order_ids (chain-shape.md line 137-145 documents the correct encoding: high bit = ask, bits 64-127 = price for asks, inverted price for bids — verify the bid decode against a real captured order_id, not the fixture builder roundtrip).

title: traverseBigVector silently swallows all per-slice fetch errors with bare catch+continue
description: Iter-2 added `try { ... } catch { continue; }` around the per-slice sui_getObject call to handle BigVector slice churn (chain-shape.md line 306-310 documents this race). The catch is bare — no error is logged, no count is kept, no signal is emitted. If ALL slices fail (e.g. RPC down, packageId wrong), traverseBigVector returns `[]` and the pool's book becomes silently empty. computeMarketStats then returns mid/spread/depth all undefined and the user sees '—' for every metric — looking identical to a genuinely empty pool.
impact: Silent total failure of book reads renders identically to a healthy idle pool. The iter-1 R3-005 'silent stub' is structurally back: same '—' rendering, same lack of signal, just one layer deeper in the stack. Operator can't distinguish 'sandbox is idle' from 'all slice fetches are failing'.
recommendation: Track failed-slice count and either log via console.warn (`'%d/%d BigVector slices failed for pool %s'`) or thread the count up so PoolCard can show a 'partial data' indicator. At minimum: `} catch (err) { failedSlices++; continue; }` plus a final guard `if (failedSlices === sliceList.data.length && sliceList.data.length > 0) throw new Error('all BigVector slices failed for ...')`.

title: resolvePoolInnerFields returns null on missing content; buildPoolInnerState then silently fabricates an empty book
description: fetchPoolStats checks `if (innerFields)` and on null falls through to `poolState = { pool_id: descriptor.poolId, book: { asks: [], bids: [], lot_size: '0', min_size: '0', tick_size: '0' } }` — a hardcoded empty book with NO error, NO log, NO signal. resolvePoolInnerFields returns null in three places (lines 113, 144 — missing content, missing wrapper) and these are all distinct failure modes (object deleted, wrong objectId, dynamic-field traversal failure) that the user has zero visibility into. The empty-book result then flows through computeMarketStats producing mid/spread/depth all undefined — rendering '—' for every metric — which looks identical to either an idle pool or a successfully-read empty pool.
impact: Same silent-empty pattern as R3-015 but at the outer level: a pool object that exists but is mid-upgrade, has been deleted, or whose wrapper shape has drifted produces '—' across the board with no operator-visible distinction from 'no orders on book'. AC1.1's 'inline error UI' goal is bypassed entirely for this path. Worse: this is the explicit 'else' branch of the error path the silent-failure-hunter rubric targets — the dev WROTE the fallback knowing the fields might be missing, but never decided what the user should see.
recommendation: Either throw with an actionable message ('Pool ${descriptor.poolId} inner state unreadable — wrapper shape mismatch or object missing') so the per-pool error banner fires, or attach a `dataState: 'ok' | 'partial' | 'empty' | 'error'` field to PoolCardData so the UI can distinguish 'genuinely empty' from 'failed to read'.

title: buildQueryEventsFn coerces timestamp via Number() with 0 fallback; malformed timestamps silently halt pagination
description: buildQueryEventsFn computes `const timestampMs = Number(j['timestamp'] ?? ev.timestampMs ?? 0)`. If both fields are missing or non-numeric, timestampMs becomes 0 (epoch). The fill is then pushed downstream with timestampMs=0, where fillFetcher's window check `nowMs - ev.timestampMs > DAY_MS` (line 67) is trivially true for nowMs > 86400000 (any modern clock), which sets `crossedWindow = true` and HALTS pagination after that page. Result: a single malformed event in a page truncates the entire fetch; subsequent in-window fills are never collected.
impact: One bad event per pool truncates that pool's fill stream. Volume24h drops to whatever was collected before the malformed event; sparkline truncates similarly. Silent: PoolCard renders the partial data without indicating it's partial. Worst case: the malformed event is the FIRST event in the descending-order response → entire pool's fill set is empty.
recommendation: Filter malformed events in buildQueryEventsFn: if the parsed timestamp is non-finite or <= 0, skip the event (don't push) AND don't let it influence pagination. Alternatively, use a more conservative default like `nowMs` so malformed events are treated as 'still in window'.

title: App.tsx setInterval refresh has no in-flight guard; slow fetches stack and overlap
description: The new periodic-refresh effect (H-5 fix) uses `setInterval(async () => { ... await Promise.allSettled(...) }, 20_000)`. setInterval does NOT wait for the previous callback to resolve before firing the next. If a fetchPoolStats batch takes >20 s (entirely possible with R3-009's unbounded pagination, R3-005's no-timeout fetch, or just slow chain reads), a second batch starts while the first is still in flight. The two batches both setState; the second-to-resolve overwrites the first. With n pools and slow fetches, in-flight requests stack indefinitely — runaway resource usage, race conditions on cachedPackageId, and stale data clobbering fresh data.
impact: Under degraded RPC conditions (sandbox under load, wifi flaky, fillFetcher hung per R3-009), the SPA accumulates background fetches indefinitely. Memory/socket pressure on the browser; on the sandbox side, multiplied RPC load can worsen the original slowness. setState ordering is non-deterministic — user may see stats flicker between fresh and stale.
recommendation: Track an in-flight ref: `const inFlightRef = useRef(false); ... if (inFlightRef.current) return; inFlightRef.current = true; try { await ... } finally { inFlightRef.current = false; }`. Or replace setInterval with a self-rescheduling setTimeout that fires the next call only after the previous resolves.

title: App.tsx refresh interval setState fires after unmount; cancelled flag not honored in interval callback
description: The setInterval callback calls `setState` unconditionally on resolution; there is no `cancelled` ref equivalent to the initial-load effect (line 42). The cleanup function clears the interval, but a callback that was already in-flight when cleanup ran will still call setState after unmount. React 19 will warn ('Cannot update state on an unmounted component') and in strict-mode dev double-invocation this fires reliably.
impact: Console-warning noise + a small leak (state of unmounted components held in closure). Low because in production the App rarely unmounts (single-route SPA), but in dev/testing the noise pollutes the AC1.1 'no console errors' goal.
recommendation: Add a `cancelled` ref shared across both effects (or a single AbortController) and guard each setState behind `if (!cancelled.current) setState(...)`.

title: main.tsx cachedPackageId race — fetchPoolStats can read empty string before loadManifest assigns it
description: main.tsx threads packageId from manifest to fetchPoolStats via a module-level `let cachedPackageId = ''`. The override of deps.loadManifest (lines 64-69) assigns cachedPackageId AFTER the original loadManifest resolves. App.tsx's useEffect awaits loadManifest before calling fetchPoolStats, so the happy path is fine — but the design is fragile: any future refactor that calls deps.fetchPoolStats without first awaiting deps.loadManifest will silently pass packageId='' to the data layer, producing JSON-RPC queries with `MoveModule.package: ''` that fail or (worse) return events from no pool.
impact: Latent fragility, no current bug. The mutation pattern (rebinding deps.loadManifest after the deps object literal is built) is clever but non-obvious; a code reader might call fetchPoolStats from a new entry point and not realise the cache must be primed first.
recommendation: Either thread packageId through the descriptor (extend PoolDescriptor to include packageId, populated in loadManifest) or hold the manifest in a Promise and await it inside fetchPoolStats. Avoid the rebinding-after-assignment pattern.

title: runDataLayer silently coerces missing packageId to empty string
description: runDataLayer's `const packageId = manifest.packages?.deepbook?.packageId ?? '';` silently coerces a missing packageId to '' rather than throwing. The downstream queryEvents call then issues `{ MoveModule: { package: '', module: 'pool' } }` which the Sui RPC will reject (invalid package id format) — error eventually surfaces, but as a confusing JSON-RPC error rather than the validated 'manifest missing packages.deepbook.packageId' error parseManifest is designed to throw. Note: when called via main.tsx, parseManifest validates first so this path is unreachable. But runDataLayer accepts a raw `manifest` object directly (RunDataLayerArgs) and is used by tests; it should validate or assume validated input.
impact: Defensive gap. Silent fallback duplicates parseManifest's responsibility but doesn't enforce it. If a future caller bypasses parseManifest (e.g. constructs a manifest object inline for testing), the empty-string packageId silently flows to the chain.
recommendation: Add an explicit assertion at the top of runDataLayer: `if (!manifest.packages?.deepbook?.packageId) throw new Error('runDataLayer: manifest missing packages.deepbook.packageId');`. Better: change the type of manifest to LoadedManifest (the validated shape) so the type system enforces it.
evidence:
const pools = manifest.pools ?? {};
  const packageId = manifest.packages?.deepbook?.packageId ?? '';
